items.title: Baldwin Lee’s Unseen New York
items.content:
Before the South, there was New York. And before the portraits, the vast emptiness of its architectural structures. Born in 1951, Baldwin Lee grew up in Manhattan’s Chinatown. He first studied under Minor White, a presiding figure of contemplative photography, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, before going on to Yale, where Walker Evans’s teaching — Evans being the undisputed reference of American documentary photography — completed the formation of his eye. “I would tell my students that my photography teachers, White and Evans, were the equivalent of having studied with Matisse and Cézanne,” he recalls in an interview with Jessica Bell Brown published in Baldwin Lee (Hunters Point Press, 2022).

After graduating in 1975, he returned again and again to the city of his childhood, a 4×5 view camera on a tripod over his shoulder, moving through Manhattan at dawn, often in winter, when the sidewalks emptied of their inhabitants. “My trips to New York City from New England were an exploration of buildings as organic forms,” the artist confides. “Rather than approaching the work as architectural photography, I saw it as a way of capturing a landscape. It was my first time using a large-format camera. Early in the morning, with no one around, I felt an overwhelming intimacy — as if I were walking through my own private garden.”

His subjects include Wall Street at dawn, Times Square, and the streets and vacant lots of Lower Manhattan where the World Trade Center looms in the distance. Baldwin Lee records a city suspended between neglect and ambition, where remnants of the past remain visible alongside the structures of the new. Worn brick facades, Cadillac Eldorados parked along the curb, the twin towers still new: these images carry the trace of a human presence temporarily absent but not gone. “If the buildings were people it would be acceptable if they did not speak,” he tells Blind. “The silence can be a metaphor for spaces, once occupied, now vacant. The lack of people points to an unfulfilled potential.”


Baldwin Lee went on to teach at Yale, then at the Massachusetts College of Art. In 1982, he moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, where he founded the photography program at the university, which he would lead for more than thirty years. The following year, he embarked on an extensive series of journeys through the American South. Between 1983 and 1989, he made nearly ten thousand photographs, principally of Black communities — a body of work celebrated as a major social testament to rural Black America. “The photographs I made in the South would never have come about without adequate education and awareness: North/South, Black/white, male/female, private/public, poor/rich, powerful/subjugated,” he tells Jessica Bell Brown.

The New York photographs reveal a different but related aspect of Baldwin Lee’s practice. Their careful organization of architectural space and sustained attention to the character of place helped establish the distinctive visual language he would carry into his later work. They demonstrate a sensitivity to form and order, but also to the humanity inscribed in the built environment. His vision of New York is a record of what people made, inhabited, altered, and left behind.

The prints selected for the exhibition present his images at a scale he has never seen before. “No, I have not seen them printed at that scale,” he confides to Blind. “At this large scale the photographs and the viewer have a different relationship. A dialog between the photograph is possible and encouraged. The viewer is now capable of entering the space of the photo making for a more intimate experience.”

The twin towers that dominate several of his images have since vanished from the New York sky. The city Baldwin Lee once photographed as his own private garden no longer exists.

“Baldwin Lee: New York (1975–1979)” is on show at the Howard Greenberg Gallery from September 18, 2026 to October 31, 2026.

A reception with the artist will be held at the Howard Greenberg Gallery on Thursday, September 17, 2026 from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m.

Baldwin Lee is published by Hunters Point Press (2022).

items.title: Will Vogt: “People Are Rarely As Buttoned-Up As They Appear”
items.content:
In America, fortune is often written in the plural of houses. Will Vogt owns three, which have also served as his hunting grounds as a photographer: a home in Corpus Christi, on the Texas Gulf coast; the family ranch, also in Texas; and, in Watch Hill, Rhode Island, the summer house where his family has gathered — and let themselves be photographed — for generations.

The boy he once was grew up elsewhere, in Haverford, Pennsylvania. More drawn to books than to sport, he discovered F. Scott Fitzgerald at boarding school, fell for his hero, Gatsby, and received his first camera not long after. From then on, it was his own world he turned the lens toward.

More than 70,000 images later, Will Vogt is far more than a chronicler of American wealth. His debut, These Americans, published in 2023, sold out. Three years later, Behind the Hedges returns to the same rituals — epic hunts, grand weddings, private society rallies — but the snapshot has given way to something more composed, and the urgency of youth to something more restrained. Interview.


Your previous book, These Americans, caught the moment. Behind the Hedges, your new book, composes it into tableaux. In practical terms, what changed in the way you shoot and sequence images between the two books?

Will Vogt: I’m not sure that the way I shoot changed as much as my material has. The advent of digital photography has also allowed me to capture more detail, which in turn makes larger tableau images possible.

These Americans drew heavily from photographs I took in the 1980s when I was younger and life around me was moving pretty fast. Behind the Hedges returns to many of the same people, places and traditions thirty years later. I’m older as are many of my subjects and as a result the pictures have slowed down a little too.

What did change enormously was my understanding of editing and sequencing. Before working with Jennifer Garza-Cuen on These Americans, I really had no idea how a photography book was put together. I learned that it isn’t a collection of your best photographs. In a book, the individual images have to work together, create a rhythm and tell a story.

In Behind the Hedges, your frame often leans on the natural or built architecture of a setting: a leading line draws the eye toward the façade of Lainston House, table and chairs arranged in the foreground; elsewhere, a swimming pool fills the foreground of the image. What place does aesthetic hold in your work?

Will Vogt: A very important one. I may be documenting something but I still want to make great photographs. I’ve always been conscious of composition, light and the relationship between people and the places they inhabit.

The surroundings are also part of the story. A house, a swimming pool, a shooting field or a dining room tells you something about the people in the photograph before you know anything about them. Sometimes the setting is every bit as important as the people.

In the essay he wrote to accompany These Americans, novelist Jay McInerney, author of Bright Lights, Big City, says “there’s no pane of glass” between you and your subjects. Doesn’t that closeness encroach on the distance a photographer sometimes needs from his subject?

Will Vogt: Familiarity gives me great access, but more than that it allows people to be comfortable around me and the camera. That is a tremendous advantage.

I think that is where the photographer has to create his own distance. You’re part of the scene but you’re also removed enough to document it. I’ve been doing that for most of my adult life, so I don’t think about it very consciously anymore.


One photograph in Behind the Hedges shows nothing but the filthy window of a Range Rover, finger-written with the line: “I wish my wife was as dirty as this.” The gap between a message that crude and a world that buttoned-up seems to delight you, as though you were forever hunting for the grain of sand that might jam the machine…

Will Vogt: I do like that photograph and particularly the contradiction and the humor. I don’t think I’m hunting for something to jam the machine. I’m looking for things that make the picture more complicated and thought-provoking than what you might expect.

There are plenty of preconceived ideas about this world and photographs like that one upset those expectations a little. People are rarely as buttoned-up as they appear. That’s what makes them interesting to photograph.

Behind the Hedges opens on a quote from F. Scott Fitzgerald, as an epigraph, before the first photograph. What place does literature hold in your eye as a photographer?

Will Vogt: I’ve always read a lot and I’m certainly attracted to writers who are good observers of people and social worlds. I fell in love with the writing of F. Scott Fitzgerald as a boy, about the same time I started taking pictures. He understood that wealth and privilege could be both seductive and complicated. I think I have documented some of that in my own work.

When I’m taking a photograph, I’m not thinking about Fitzgerald or trying to make an image look literary. Those connections tend to emerge later. A photograph can contain a whole story without explaining it. In that sense, I suppose photography and literature have quite a lot in common.

Behind the Hedges returns again and again to scenes of killing: a pit of zebra carcasses, partridges hung in neat rows, hares laid out on moss. What do these scenes of slaughter reveal, in your view, about this supposedly well-mannered society?

Will Vogt: I probably wouldn’t use the word slaughter. Hunting has been a large part of my life and of the world I photograph. Those images are part of the reality of it. I don’t see a reason to sanitize that reality by showing the shooting party and leaving out the dead game.

There is also a long tradition surrounding hunting, particularly in England and South Texas. The game, the land, the dogs, the people and the rituals surrounding all of it are connected. I photograph what is there and leave it to the viewer to decide what he or she thinks about it.

The English photographer Martin Parr, who died in December 2025, spent his life photographing the British middle and working classes and their mass leisure — but as an observer, from outside that world, with an eye that was affectionate and often satirical. You do the opposite: you’ve always photographed the American elite you were born into, from the inside. Do you feel any kinship with him nonetheless?

Will Vogt: Absolutely. I have always admired Martin Parr’s work. We came at our subjects from slightly different angles but I think we shared an interest in the small details that tell you something larger about people and the way they live.

Parr was brilliant at noticing things that other people walked right past. His photographs could be funny without simply making fun of people. I hope there is some of that observational quality in my work.


Jennifer Garza-Cuen, the editor of Behind the Hedges, places your work alongside Larry Sultan, Stephen Shore and Tod Papageorge. What did you take from each of them, and what shows up from those influences in your own eye?

Will Vogt: Those three photographers are masters of their craft and I am honored that anyone would mention me in the same sentence with them. Robert Frank was obviously the earliest and most important influence on my work. I have collected photographs and photography books for many years and inevitably some of what I’ve absorbed has become part of the way I see and photograph the world.

If someone opened Behind the Hedges knowing nothing about you and decided it was satire, what would you tell them?

Will Vogt: I’d tell them they are entitled to see it that way. Once you put photographs into the world, you lose control over how people interpret them.

But satire isn’t my intention. I’m not trying to celebrate these people and I’m not trying to ridicule them. I’m recording a world I know and have been part of for my entire life. There is humor in the photographs because there is humor in life. There are also contradictions and occasionally absurdity. I don’t think you have to manufacture any of that. You just have to notice it.

As a teenager, you saw Jimi Hendrix live — a world at the opposite end of the one you’ve been photographing ever since. You also cite the Beatles and Bob Dylan among your influences. Doesn’t that irreverent spirit find its extension in the way you photograph high society — as a bit of a troublemaker yourself?

Will Vogt: I like the idea of being a troublemaker, although I’m not sure I’ve earned the title.

Music was a huge influence on me when I was young and still is. Hendrix, Dylan and the Beatles all arrived at a time when a lot of accepted ideas about how you were supposed to live were being challenged. I was certainly affected by that.

Maybe some of that does show up in the photographs. I’ve never felt any obligation to make this world look the way it might like to see itself. If something is funny, strange, awkward or a little outrageous, I’m probably going to take the picture. Maybe that is my small contribution to troublemaking.

“Will Vogt: These Americans” runs through December 6, 2026 at the Art Museum of South Texas.

items.title: Stacy Kranitz: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Wounds
items.content:
“I don’t believe in ending stories. I just don’t do it.” Stacy Kranitz drops the line by Lake Geneva, on the afternoon of the Images Vevey Book Award ceremony, between two questions about swimming. Seventeen years she has been working in Appalachia, the mountain range that runs more than 3,000 kilometers from Canada down to Alabama. Or twenty, she hesitates. The book takes its title from a gospel song by Brother Claude Ely, a Pentecostal preacher from those mountains. The jury chaired by Rineke Dijkstra crowned it; Éditions Images Vevey and the American publisher Terrible Baby brought it out in June. One idea governs the whole: every image manufactures a little of the reputation it claims to describe.

At the Musée Jenisch, the installation applies that principle to the letter. Stacy Kranitz’s color photographs, made in a West Virginia hollow, face the images produced about the region by outsiders since 1850. Missionaries raising funds, photographers on the payroll of the coal companies, envoys of the Farm Security Administration, reporters covering the War on Poverty: each wave arrived with its commission in hand and its framing already written. And a documentary film directed by the photographer holds the center of the display. “There’s no visual literacy in America,” she says. “Nobody knows, understands, or processes how images circulate in the world, the different kinds of apparatuses that are at play. Nobody thinks about this stuff.”

It all starts on a Friday night in 2013, in West Columbia, West Virginia. Stacy Kranitz is invited for a beer at the home of a man who, within the hour, gets into three fistfights, throws chairs and punches his friend Dozer in the face. On the back of his neck, a tattoo: “Honkey.” The lawyer Harry Caudill would have filed Pat Greene among what he called the “dullards” of the back hollows. The photographer, for her part, keeps coming back for a decade, then another. “To me, he really identifies as a mountaineer,” she says of her host. “He really embodies the idea of living mountain life.”

One late summer, on a strip mine reclaimed as an ATV trail, Stacy Kranitz climbs on behind Dozer, camera on her back, after a dozen beers for him. The caption of one picture in the book says the rest: “Stacy and Dozer on his four-wheeler, the moment before it flipped.” Dozer, 95 kilos, lands on her; the quad, 340 kilos, lands on Dozer. One bruised elbow. Back at Pat’s, someone hands her a crushed Lortab to snort for the pain. Participant as much as observer, she photographs from inside the circle, with the risks that implies and the standing it earns.

Then comes the long history, the one the book unfolds through documents. Families left Europe to escape a class system, found themselves indentured, climbed into the mountains and lived a century outside capitalism. Then coal climbed up after them. “They literally stole the land,” Stacy Kranitz says. “They didn’t know they needed to have deeds. Nobody told them they need to have deeds. So who decides that they need to have deeds? The coal companies.” On April 24, 1964, Lyndon Johnson sat on the porch of Tom Fletcher, an unemployed miner in Inez, Kentucky, who had earned about 400 dollars the previous year. The picture became the emblem of the War on Poverty. Fletcher died poor in 2004, worn out by the reporters who came back every ten years to ask whether he still was. At the end of the volume, a “lexicon of dispossession” lines up the words coined to keep these people outside the human contract, from waste people to trailer trash. Four centuries of vocabulary, a single function.

Then there is Harry Caudill, the dark heart of the affair and the subject of the film. His essay “The Rape of the Appalachians,” published in The Atlantic in 1962, and Night Comes to the Cumberlands a year later, turned America’s attention to a region bled dry by coal. Twenty years on, the same man explained poverty by genetics, invited the eugenicist William Shockley to his Kentucky home and floated cash bounties for sterilization. Stacy Kranitz unearthed the footage in which he makes that claim on camera. On November 29, 1990, facing Pine Mountain, Caudill shot himself; his farewell letter is reproduced in the book. One detail from the same archive amuses his Swiss publishers. “He mentions the Swiss. He says, we want to do it like the Swiss,” the photographer reports. The film, for its part, turns back on its own author and asks the question that holds for the entire project: what does an image of poverty do, once it is loose in the world?

Next comes J. D. Vance, whose Hillbilly Elegy (2016) recounts an Appalachian childhood and hands his own people the blame for their decline. Stacy Kranitz places the two men in the same frame and notes the coincidence: Pat’s daughter was taken by child protective services just as Vance was named running mate. “It’s my form of politics,” she says of that montage. “I don’t know why we’re not talking about eugenics more. We are still lurking in that conversation in every direction.” A Nieman Fellow, she is spending the year at Harvard, where she studies eugenics and pronatalism.

The book saves its most troubling object for last. In 2016, a photograph of Pat shirtless in his yard became a meme: “Poor southern conservatives have been voting Republican for generations. And they’re still poor.” Pat, with a criminal record, cannot vote. The essayist Whitney Phillips devotes one of the book’s texts to it. Stacy Kranitz has known the mechanism since 2012, when CNN ran her images of a Pentecostal snake handler and a Ku Klux Klan gathering under the headline “Everyday life in Appalachia.” It took a week on the phone to get the headline changed. “Photography has done a lot of harm to that region,” she says. “That doesn’t mean that you can’t or shouldn’t.” She describes the model that governs the news: “A flood, an earthquake, some disaster, we descend on the region, everyone’s there at the same time, and then we abandon ship.” Her work does the opposite, slowly. “Art allowed me to slow down and tell the story over a much longer period of time. You can’t really do it in journalism.”

So she stays. Stacy Kranitz went through every caption with Pat Greene, recorder on the table. “I really needed him to see what I wrote,” she says, “to make sure that he agreed with the context, with the way that it was being used in the book.” The last pictures date from March 2026. As the book went to press, Pat was in jail, with no one to post bail. “We love to put poor people in jail for no good reason,” she says. Five weeks of silence, then a rehab center, where she was able to visit him. “I’ve never seen him more contemplative,” says the photographer, who has always known him in survival mode. The book ends in the dark; life has turned since. Such is the advantage of stories that keep going. “I will probably be there for a long time, and I will not be leaving.”

Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down by Stacy Kranitz is published by Terrible Baby / Éditions Images Vevey and available for $70. The exhibition at the Musée Jenisch, part of the Images Vevey Biennial, runs through September 27, 2026.

items.title: Vic Bakin: Fading
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Vic Bakin: Fading

In Materia, his second book following the monograph Epitome, Kyiv-based photographer Vic Bakin sets images against the decay of their own physical support.

 

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Vic Bakin

This work began with two portraits of the same man, made ten years apart. Bakin printed these and other portraits, together with interiors and details hinting at lingering moments, on discontinued photographic paper from the 1960s to the 2000s. Each batch aged differently: faded, spotted with mold or marked by fingerprints.

The paper’s decay seems to mirror the vulnerability of the skin. Fragility, desire, and the relentless pull of time all surface from the same image. As Bakin puts it: “For me, thinking happens through making. I rarely begin with a clear concept. Instead, I make pictures first and then spend months trying to understand what they are telling me.”

The book Materia is published by VOID and available for 60 Euro.

items.title: The Brazenness of Bangkok’s Street Youth
items.content:
The photography of Chardchakaj Waikawee, born in Bangkok in 1980, resists easy classification. It belongs neither to social documentary, with its cool rigor, nor to art portraiture, with its aestheticizing restraint. It is something else, something harder to name, and therefore more precious. His work has traveled internationally for more than fifteen years. “Youth”, the exhibition devoted to him by London’s Graces Mews, brings together a body of analog photographs taken between 2008 and 2020.

The title borrows the Thai phrase wai run, a term that reaches far beyond its literal translation to describe an inner disposition, an energy of being that neither age nor poverty can extinguish. Waikawee’s subjects include motorcycle-taxi drivers, street vendors, and more broadly the young people who survive on the margins of Bangkok’s economy. “Bangkok is chaos,” he says. “Heaven and hell exist on the same street.”

One enters the exhibition through a filmed portrait of the photographer, his voice continuing to murmur through the galleries like an undertow. This sonic device anchors the images in a meditation on memory, time and value: sober words for photographs that are anything but. For Waikawee’s eye plays as much as it bears witness. One need only look at the boy sipping Coca-Cola from a plastic bag, staring straight into the lens with quiet defiance, to be convinced of it. Or the punk whose extravagant pink mohawk bursts through the open sunroof of a champagne-colored Mercedes.

What strikes one, technically, is the deliberate insolence of the process. Waikawee works with expired film, repaired cameras, hand-printing techniques. Cross-processing produces unpredictable chromatic shifts — lemon yellow, scorched orange, acid magenta — which the photographer treats as so many traces of time’s passage upon the material itself. The scratches, the dust, the chemical marks are not accidents but the visible memory of the making, a reminder that every image is also a physical object.

Full of life, these portraits are anything but miserabilist. “Each image reflects a relationship before it becomes a photograph,” Waikawee notes. He foregrounds the personality, the friendship, the singular sense of style of his subjects, who wear their appearance as armor against the social and economic invisibility the city imposes upon them.

Take the laborers crammed into the back of a truck, riding home at night in a tableau at once baroque and entirely ordinary. Or the boy whose back, tattooed with sacred Sak Yant script, is covered in inscriptions down to the waistband of his jeans. One will long remember, too, the doll-like face of the young woman, her eyes lined in black, holding the camera’s gaze without flinching. So many ways, for this sidelined but defiant youth, to compose, with whatever means are to hand, a presence in the world.

“Youth”, by Chardchakaj Waikawee, runs until 19 September 2026 at Graces Mews, London.
items.excerpt: In the portraits of Chardchakaj Waikawee, Thailand’s marginalized youth astonish with sheer presence.

items.title: Images Vevey: Families, I Love You
items.content:
“Families, I hate you!” thundered André Gide in 1897, in Fruits of the Earth. More than a century later, on the shore of Lake Geneva, the sentiment has flipped. Families, I love you, then, and set to music: for the tenth edition of the biennial he founded in 2008, Stefano Stoll drew his theme from Sister Sledge, “We Are Family,” the obligatory soundtrack of weddings and christenings, which entered the Grammy Hall of Fame the very year Images Vevey was born (fate has a sense of humor). Beneath the disco ball, an idea. “It’s precisely within families that you learn nuance, that you learn to live together”, the director argues, “to get worked up at the uncle who isn’t on your side of the political fence at Christmas.” By March, he adds, you can see him again, at the cousin’s wedding. A lesson in domestic diplomacy.

Visitors stepping off the train are met at once by a familiar face. On Place de la Gare, Martin Parr sits among the flowers, while behind him Alice, the daughter of Siân Davey, waves a balloon. The English photographer, who died in December 2025, appears in “The Garden”, Siân Davey’s series about a wild garden opened to neighbors, loved ones and passersby. An elegant detour, dictated by house rule: Images Vevey shows only living artists. “We’ve never done deceased people, we’ve never done what would have made life easier for us, certainly”, Stefano Stoll admits. “But we like complicated things.” Martin Parr, who never missed a chance to sing the biennial’s praises, would surely have relished the twist.

On the Grande Place, between the Grenette and the Bois d’Amour, Barbara Davatz unfurls an open-air family tree. A masterwork of patience. In 1982, in a Zurich still electrified by youth riots, the Swiss photographer, born in 1944, had 12 couples of lovers, friends or relatives pose in her studio, facing the camera against a plain grey backdrop, shot on a large-format camera in black and white. She started again in 1988, in 1997 and in 2014, with the same subjects, their new partners, their children, soon their grandchildren. Three generations, 14 children swelling the ranks, couples forming and dissolving, hairstyles that date each decade more reliably than carbon-14. The protocol stays identical; only the faces change. Davatz calls it her “photographic family”, and this year, the phrase lands perfectly. “Every picture is the record of a relationship, the sum of the pictures is a record of time”, the artist sums up. A record you walk through here in a few steps, decade to decade, scanning the faces for who stayed, who left, who arrived.

Back toward the station, in the former railway workers’ housing, L’Appartement lives up to its name. Richard Billingham marks the 30th anniversary of Ray’s a Laugh, published in 1996 by the Zurich publisher Walter Keller (Scalo), a book Stefano Stoll discovered in London in 1997, at the “Sensation” exhibition, where his parents had taken him. In the family, inevitably. “All of a sudden I understood that Richard’s parents, Liz and Ray, actually lived in two separate apartments”, he recalls. Two towers of the same council estate, in Margaret Thatcher’s England. Liz leaves with Jason, the younger brother; Ray stays with Richard for four years, living on his notorious “home-brewed beer”, until she agrees to take him back, the alcoholic, on condition that he stops drinking. The show follows that geography: on one side, Liz’s flat; on the other, Ray’s, where unpublished black-and-white prints show one man and his room. Further on, the film Fishtank (1998) plays in a room wallpapered to match. “We were like fish in a tank”, Richard Billingham once told the director, who draws his own moral from it: “We, in our tidy Swiss households, learn to live with very little chaos. In the end, chaos is life.”

At Château de l’Aile, where not a single nail is allowed, Vik Muniz reassembles, from thousands of photographs picked up at flea markets, everything a family album contains: the children’s birthdays, the parents’ wedding, mom at the beach, the first bike. A few rooms further, a change of dynasty. In the room next door, Cristina De Middel, whose very first exhibition took place in Vevey back in 2010, hangs “Endofgamia”, a title that fuses endogamy and endgame. It began as a Prado commission: the artist selected the royal-family galleries, the Spanish Habsburgs first among them, and superimposed the portraits, keeping the eyes in the same place. “It created a kind of monster where you can still recognize the family’s distinctive features”, she says (the Habsburg chin has never looked so collective). The museum balked. “They didn’t like it”, De Middel recalls, “because it was a bit critical of the royal family, and we were in a kingdom, after all.” Printed on a metallic, reflective surface, these hybrid faces seem to follow visitors with their gaze, as in a haunted château. “If you don’t like the show, it’s too late now, Cristina”, Stefano Stoll tells the artist, freshly arrived from Brazil to discover an installation designed remotely. Family humor.

Time passing, again. At the Musée de la Confrérie des Vignerons, guardian of a festival held every 25 years, “once a generation”, Rineke Dijkstra, a fixture of the world’s great museums, agreed to be shown “in pocket format”, as Stefano Stoll puts it. In “Almerisa”, her longest-running series, a young Bosnian girl photographed in 1994, aged five, in a refugee center in Leiden, returns over the years, always seated on the same chair. At first, her feet don’t reach the floor. The final portrait, taken in 2024, is shown here for the first time. In the guild’s historic hall, the video “Marianna (The Fairy Doll)” follows a 10-year-old girl repeating her audition for ballet school under her teacher’s sharp instructions, in Russian. A hard school.

Above, visitors climb to the attic of the Musée historique, ordinarily closed to the public, for “Shades of Time 2.0”. “Twenty-five years ago, we were all captivated by this installation”, Stefano Stoll recalls. Annelies Štrba, born in 1947 in Zug, runs through four generations of her family: the house at Melide on Lake Lugano, sleeping children, the kitchen, then the places marked by disaster where her travels led her, Chernobyl, Hiroshima, Kobe. The book, published in 1997 by Lars Müller, became a landmark. In 2020, the artist re-edited the whole sequence digitally, with sound, the old-fashioned way, image after image. It brings to mind Nan Goldin’s The Ballad of Sexual Dependency, relocated to the shores of Ticino: the same hypnotic scroll, the same music holding lives together, and the same tenderness for ordinary days. The slideshow has never before been shown in French-speaking Switzerland (the Röstigraben dies hard). “It’s also wonderful to be able to show this to a generation that’s starting to get hooked on artificial intelligence”, the director adds.

A major figure of the Mexican scene, who represented his country at the Venice Biennale in 2017, Carlos Amorales “isn’t really into photography”, Stefano Stoll admits, having met him on every visit to Mexico City. Except in 1996. As a student in Amsterdam, he invented Los Amorales, a lucha libre alter ego wearing a mask cast from his own face, in a culture where the mask is sacred: “a wrestler never removes his mask, on pain of losing his entire career”, the director notes. Long reluctant to reopen that chapter, the artist gave in for the 30th anniversary. During a month-long residency at La Becque, he selected 150 slides out of hundreds and animated them with artificial intelligence: his girlfriend at the time, the bouts, his own family. At the Théâtre Oriental, a mosaic of raw photographs answers the film. On one side, memory as it was; on the other, as a machine dreams it. Poignant. Artist and father, Carlos Amorales delivers a self-portrait thirty years apart, “a time trip through today’s technology”, says Stefano Stoll. The biennial has thought of everything, down to a label modeled on allergen warnings: “May contain traces of AI”.

Another liturgy: football. At the Cinéma Astor, Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait plays on loop, free of charge. On April 23, 2005, Douglas Gordon and Philippe Parreno trained 17 cameras on the Real Madrid number 5 as he faced Villarreal, from kickoff to the final red card, set to a score by Mogwai. “Football is something that unites nations and families, and just as much divides nations and families”, Stefano Stoll notes, having brought in amateur football media so that sports fans and art lovers could share the same stand. Another video worth a look: at the church of Sainte-Claire, a small screen in a large nave is all Ange Leccia needs to slow down John Travolta in Saturday Night Fever and swap the Bee Gees for Eartha Kitt. “I still felt I was missing something with a bit of grit to it”, the director of Images Vevey admits. On Rue d’Italie, Erika Stucky, queen of jazz-inflected yodel, unveils 44 years of photographs projected behind her at concerts, her blood family and her musical family alike, starting with her first Instamatic snapshot: her parents, nudists. Surprise concerts at 1:13 p.m. and 3:15 p.m. during opening weekend. “She asked us to find her a snow shovel”, Stefano Stoll notes, for the sound effects.

No family escapes grief, says a Chinese proverb Stefano Stoll has made his own. At the Jardin de l’Oyonne, on Quai Roussy, Deanna Dikeman says goodbye, for 27 years running. In 1991, leaving her parents’ home in Sioux City, Iowa, the American photographer shot their wave from her car. The gesture became a ritual. Seasons turn, the photographer’s son grows from a car seat to the driver’s seat, the father disappears from the frame in 2009, days after his 91st birthday, the mother carries on alone, then waves from the doorway of an assisted-living facility, until her death in October 2017. The final photograph: the empty driveway. “For the first time in my life, no one was waving back at me”, Deanna Dikeman writes. The staging, one of a kind, unrolls the chronology, goodbye after goodbye. A crowd favorite in 2022, the installation returns with exactly the same structure, simply relocated to a different garden. Stefano Stoll hopes visitors will say to themselves, “I’ve seen this before, but it wasn’t here, not like this”. Déjà vu, yes, but the same lump in the throat.

Another grief, another scale. Erik Kessels, who once filled a Vevey church with 350,000 images, returns with a single one. That of his sister Susan, struck by a car at nine, when he was 11: the last photograph his parents could find of her, taken in an amusement park. “One Image” spreads unlabeled through the shop windows of Vevey, on billboards, in the press, and explains itself in only one place, on the façade of the Salle del Castillo. A blow to the chest. On Place de l’Hôtel de Ville, Sunil Gupta stages a demonstration: the London marches of 1985 to 1995 against Section 28, the 1988 law that barred schools from presenting homosexuality as a “pretended family relationship” (Margaret Thatcher, an uninvited guest at two exhibitions). At the Salle del Castillo, “Lovers, Revisited”, made with his husband Charan Singh, shows queer couples at home. “Does a gay couple at home make a family? You all have your own answer, but the fact remains it’s still far from a given”, Stefano Stoll observes.

At the Musée Jenisch, which brings together the Grand Prix laureates, Amandine Marchand, in charge of Éditions Images Vevey, leads visitors into an unusual shop. “Undercover Pleasures” takes its name from the sex shop Pacifico Silano’s parents ran in New Jersey when he was a teenager. The American artist, born in 1986 and awarded a special mention, evokes its interior and builds collages from gay erotic magazines of the 1970s and 1980s, pages simply laid one over the other. It all starts from an absence: his uncle, who died of AIDS, erased from the family albums by shame. “Growing up, I only had one Polaroid of my uncle”, Pacifico Silano told BOMB magazine in 2024. The installation also honors his mother, devoted to her own. The family album gets its torn-out pages back. Same museum, another lineage of men: Abdulhamid Kircher, a Grand Prix laureate, studies Turkish oil wrestlers, a tradition dating to the 14th century and practiced within his father’s family, caught between virility and tenderness. Stacy Kranitz, winner of the Book Prize, sets nearly 20 years of photographs of Appalachia against the archives that built the region’s poor reputation (read our dedicated article).

Objects, too, have their family stories. Facing the lake, near the Alimentarium, once Nestlé’s headquarters, Tokuko Ushioda lines up eight diptychs, the fridge closed, the fridge open, photographed in Tokyo households between 1981 and 1995. Brillat-Savarin, appliance edition. “Tell me how you keep your fridge, tell me what you eat, and I’ll tell you what kind of family you are”, Stefano Stoll jokes, throat lozenges in his pocket to save his voice before singing that same evening. “It’s one of the last places you show to friends.” Mark Wallinger, by contrast, isolates. Inside a former fast-food outlet (“not Starbucks, Subway”, the director corrects), six anonymous city dwellers turn in circles in front of a large mirror. “You can have 1,000 people walking down the Champs-Élysées, and you still have 1,000 isolated individuals”, Stefano Stoll observes.

Last stop, the Salle del Castillo. JR, whose monumental 2010 and 2012 projects helped Images Vevey “take off”, in Stefano Stoll’s words, marks the 15th anniversary of “Inside Out” here. Vevey was one of the project’s first international stops: 5,200 portraits shot in three weeks, back in 2012. Two cubes face each other. In the first, the faces of 2012; in the second, those of 2026, taken that very morning in a mobile photo booth and pasted up as fast as they came in by the crew. Visitors look for someone, maybe Valérie, and find an artist, a neighbor, an elected official, or themselves 15 years younger. “You are the ones who pushed us to become who we are”, Stefano Stoll says, before concluding, in front of the still-fresh posters: “Family is you.”

Images Vevey Biennial, “We are family!,” 10th edition, September 5–27, 2026, Vevey (Switzerland). Some fifty projects, free of charge; indoor exhibitions open daily from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.

items.title: The Last Pictures Taken Inside the World Trade Center
items.content:
IN IMAGES

The Last Pictures Taken Inside the World Trade Center

In the summer of 2001, a night-shift electrician wandered the empty floors of the World Trade Center with a digital camera, photographing offices, kitchens and stairwells no one else thought to record. Twenty-five years later, for the anniversary of September 11, Blind publishes this set of historical images.

 

By Jonas Cuénin. Photos by Konstantin Petrov.

Konstantin Petrov arrived in New York from Estonia in 1998, working unlicensed electrical jobs before he landed steadier work. In June 2001, he took a night-shift position at Windows on the World, the restaurant occupying the 106th and 107th floors of the North Tower. By day he was the superintendent of a Manhattan apartment building; by night, alone in the towers after the offices emptied out, he carried his camera.

Over that summer he shot hundreds of digital photographs: banquettes and table settings laid for the next day’s service, elevator fixtures, sconces, stairwells, kitchen equipment. From more than 1,300 feet up, his eye also caught dawn breaking over a dormant Manhattan, the city visible through glass no one else was looking through at that hour.

Petrov shared the images on Fotki, an early Estonian photo-sharing site started by his friend Dmitri Don. “World Trade Center is, like, so cool,” Don later recalled the two of them saying when Petrov got the job, a line he still gave years afterward, once the towers were gone and the remark had taken on a different weight.

On the morning of September 11, Petrov finished his shift and drove out of the building’s basement parking garage. He was already gone when the first plane struck, and didn’t grasp what had happened until he reached home and turned on the news.

The photographs sat unnoticed until 2014, when documentary filmmaker Erik Nelson, researching a National Geographic film called 9/10: The Final Hours, found Petrov’s Fotki archive and used 44 of the images. Petrov never saw that recognition: he died in a motorcycle accident on Manhattan’s West Side Highway in 2002, less than a year after the attacks.

Konstantin Petrov’s photographs remain one of the only interior records of the World Trade Center from its final months, empty rooms and quiet views taken by someone with no reason to think they would matter. Twenty-five years later, they stand on their own: a night-shift electrician’s private archive, published now as the last look inside a building that no longer exists.

items.title: Women Photographers Steal the Spotlight
items.content:
Hundred Heroines, devoted to promoting and championing women photographers, begins with an observation that has long gone unaddressed: behind the greatest portraits of twentieth-century stars, there was almost always a woman behind the lens. Its ambition is to restore these women to the centre of photographic history — a history they helped write, from which they have too often been erased.

For the earliest works in the show, Hundred Heroines has partnered with Sisters of the Lens, an organisation dedicated to promoting women photographers who worked between the 1850s and 1960s, which has made rare original prints available for this exhibition.

Three unjustly forgotten pioneers are brought back into the light: Lallie Charles, an Irish photographer based in London and one of the most celebrated society portraitists of the Edwardian era: Dorothy Wilding, the first woman appointed as Official Royal Photographer to the British Crown, whose portraits of Elizabeth II appeared on UK postage stamps; and Madame D’Ora, an Austrian photographer who established herself first in Vienna, then in Paris from 1925 onwards, as one of the defining portraitists of fashion and high society in the first half of the twentieth century.

These pioneers immortalized, among others, the British actress Vivien Leigh, whom the world first encountered in Gone with the Wind (1939), the blazing American entertainer Tallulah Bankhead, and the German-American star Marlene Dietrich, the supreme icon of pre-war cinema.

South African photographer Jillian Edelstein, born in Cape Town and based in London since the 1980s, dominates the contemporary section of the exhibition. Trained in photojournalism and published in the New York Times Magazine and Vogue, she pursues in every portrait “the humanity behind the mask of celebrity, the person behind the persona.”

Among Edelstein’s most powerful images is her portrait of the late British punk fashion designer Vivienne Westwood, who died in 2022, shot with her wild flame-orange hair and two small silver horns tucked into her curls, her expression poised somewhere between mischief and majesty. Amy Winehouse, the prodigiously gifted British soul and jazz singer who died at 27 in 2011, appears with arms folded and gaze averted — at once an icon and a raw, exposed soul.

The archive of Elisabeth Buchmeyer-Lewis, a British photographer specializing in the music world of the late twentieth century, provides an electric counterpoint. Her images plunge into the backstage world of British rock and jazz of the 1970s and 1980s: Ian Dury, singer, lyricist and founder of the Blockheads, hunched over his microphone at the legendary 100 Club on Oxford Street, alongside previously unseen photographs of American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan and British hard rock band Led Zeppelin, captured at close range from the stage.

Taken together, these portraits measure the full extent of what women photographers gave to pop culture, and to the century that consumed it. “Stardust” puts the record straight.

“Stardust: 100 Years of Stage, Screen and Celebrity” by Hundred Heroines is on view at the new Hundred Heroines Photo Museum in Nailsworth, Gloucestershire, UK, from 11 September to 20 November 2026. Free admission.

items.title: An Instrument Called Photography
items.content:
One photograph can hide another. This is the very essence of Dysnomia Live, a performance born from a foundational body of work developed by Alexandre Dupeyron over several years. Evolving from a slideshow exchanged a decade ago between a photographer and a double bassist—an interaction that was tentative and almost accidental—into its current performance-based format, the duo continually pushes the dialogue between their disciplines further. In 2022, a system inspired by VJing—the practice of manipulating live video imagery borrowed from club culture and concerts—transformed the image into an instrument in its own right. It is a production of Collectif Déluge. A man stands in the dark, a triggering interface beneath his fingers. Images appear, overlap, dissolve to the rhythm of the double bass. Since then, the performance, 70 minutes long, has been staged around twenty times, at Fotografiska in Shanghai, the Blue Note in Beijing, and FRAC Méca in Bordeaux, taking on, depending on the stage, the form of dance, calligraphy, sometimes another language. “On stage, photography leaves behind its stillness to become living matter, which I manipulate in real time like an instrument in dialogue with the musicians,” says Alexandre Dupeyron.

The performance unfolds around three ontological questions: where do we come from, what are we, where are we going? “Silent Green” shifts that arc sideways, leaving behind our hubris to look at the world from within the living rather than above it. This shift draws on two photographic bodies of work. Ashes of the Future traces the paths of fire in Australia, France and the United States, where Dupeyron worked with researchers from the Rocky Mountain Research Station and the US Department of Agriculture’s Fire Lab, who study fire rather than extinguish it. Pinus Pinaster (2023) turns to pioneer plants and their capacity to recolonize damaged soil, to split through asphalt. “From dehumanized megacities to the resurgence of the wild, the performance unfolds a visual and sonic cosmogony,” Dupeyron sums up. Humanity becomes pharmakon here, both poison and cure.

Thomas Julienne reorchestrated the entire score for this new chapter. A string trio, two violins and a cello, joins the original lineup. Four new compositions were written specifically for the occasion, hovering between avant-garde jazz, post-rock and contemporary music. The composer also leads the quintet Theorem of Joy, whose album Feux was named best jazz album of 2025 by the magazine Paris Move, which praised “a radical album, not through provocation, but through grace.”

On the visual side, fifteen years of research and archival sedimentation feed the stagecraft. Alexandre Dupeyron assembles and manipulates his black-and-white photographs live, building an underground visual arc that traces our presence in the world, from its origins to the fractures of contemporary megacities. Photography acts here as an autonomous narrative engine, on equal footing with the music.

For the world premiere, on Sunday at Pioneer Works (Brooklyn), the ensemble welcomes drummer Ches Smith, a longtime collaborator of John Zorn and Marc Ribot. Rounding out the lineup are Ellinoa on vocals, Dylan Ebrahimian on violin, Julie Kim on cello, Dustin Carlson on guitar and Alix Tucou on trombone and keyboard. Each night, the sequence of images reinvents itself; there is no preset score of visuals.

The following day at Picto, the format tightens into a quartet: Dupeyron, Julienne on double bass, Ellinoa and Alix Tucou on bass trombone. Julienne pushes the double bass toward preparations and sonic friction, turning the instrument into a filter for the world’s raw pulse. A session conceived as a more intimate variation on the same dialogue.

The press has followed this journey. In French cultural magazine Télérama, Thierry Voisin writes that Thomas Julienne’s compositions tell “a story of the blue planet, from the formation of the earth to the final explosion.” For Fabien Ribery, in L’Intervalle, the performance sits “somewhere between the dark romanticism of Gérard de Nerval, the science-fiction experiments of Chris Marker and the metaphysical noir of Jean-Luc Godard’s Alphaville.”

In 2023, Dysnomia Live also received the “L’art de la reprise” prize (SACEM, ONDA, Institut Français), and Alexandre Dupeyron and Thomas Julienne are 2025 Villa Albertine laureates. This New York residency comes with cultural mediation workshops for music and art schools, in which the two artists introduce the concept of ecosophy, coined by Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss, for whom man is not at the top of the hierarchy of life but rather part of the ecosphere. A residency project is also under discussion with the Brooklyn Music School and the International Center of Photography, pairing five photographer-musician duos around an original piece. The tour continues in October at the Musée de la mer in Bordeaux.

The book Dysnomia, which gathers this same archival work, serves as the matrix for the performance: each visual chapter finds its answer in a composition by Theorem of Joy. “Through his work, Alexandre Dupeyron has built, across his series, uninterrupted conversations from which emerges the sense of a universal matter, like a black hole,” writes exhibition curator François Cheval in the book’s afterword. “A luminous energy bursts forth, like a vital source, asserting the presence of being as essence.”

items.title: Irina Rozovsky’s Balkan Wandering
items.content:
Mountain Black Heart opens on a dedication to “the miracle.” Three images follow, by way of prologue: a bedroom window opens onto a ceiling light that, at first glance, might be mistaken for a full moon. The next image catches a child mid-cartwheel in the tall grass at dusk. Then comes an apparition worthy of a fairy tale: the immaculate train of a bird, possibly a white peacock, perched at night in a tree. Irina Rozovsky sets out her terms here: joy and wonder sit alongside a muted unease, one that the darkness of night only sharpens.

But the miracle is slow to arrive: the book’s opening pages plunge us into cold. Nocturnal images follow one another, ruins mingling with barbed wire, plasterboard, planks of wood. A black cat slips past. A woman with a bandaged eye and a figure stretched out on a bare bench are photographed on public transport, bundled into their coats. Snow leaves its trace on a fur coat. Fog engulfs a dirt path lined with wire fencing, the whole scene faintly uncanny.


Nor can we tell whether it is dawn or nightfall, and the artist will not enlighten us. No image is captioned, no country named. Born in Moscow in 1981 and brought to the United States as a child in the wake of the Soviet Jewish exodus of the 1980s, Irina Rozovsky carries a diffuse cultural familiarity with the Slavic world, one born of a history she did not live through herself yet that runs through her all the same. When she is not on the road, she lives and works in Athens, Georgia, where she co-directs the photography space The Humid with her husband, the photographer Mark Steinmetz.

Her wanderings here are not, then, a return to any point of origin: the sense of remembrance these images stir has no precise object. No narrative thread holds them together. The work proceeds in fragments. Since 2014, Irina Rozovsky has kept returning to these territories — Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, Croatia, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania — in what she calls “a type of travel diary or personal journalism,” moving by rental car, bus, and train, crossing the borders of nations recently formed and re-formed.

This method has already proven itself: In One to Nothing (2009), Island in My Mind (2015), and then In Plain Air (2021) already bore its mark. This time, the artist attempts to “sketch a geography of heart and mind,” at the cost, at times, of a disquiet she does not shy away from. As with the image of a newborn laid straight on the ground, swaddled in a white onesie, surrounded by plastic bags and threadbare blankets at the foot of a tree, in the dark. Is it absolute precarity, or an ordinary campsite? Impossible to say. Irina Rozovsky’s photography is enigmatic: she withholds the key, leaving the viewer’s eye to construct, alone, whatever it believes it sees.

Menace coils itself into small details. From the book’s earliest pages, a large dog appears behind iron bars, jaws open. Further on, laminated banners hung from a tree bear the portraits of men, likely the victims of a massacre whose location and circumstances remain unnamed. A car crash follows, then the fleeting sight of a cemetery. Though the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s are never shown head-on, a tension bears down on each of these images, like a buried memory.

Elsewhere, a blonde woman at her window raises her arm in a gesture resembling a Nazi salute. Irina Rozovsky offers no comment. She saw. She kept the image. When she photographs a blond boy set down in the night grass, an albino python coiled around him, the harsh flash brings out the whiteness of the snake and of the child alike against the pitch dark. Natural empathy contends with a discomfort, muted and indefinable. It is this quality of unease that Irina Rozovsky cultivates, fascinated, she says, by “the struggle and endurance that pulses through a place damaged by history.”

From the very darkest of these pages, light also rises. A woman strokes the scruff of a brindle mastiff, an abandoned Soviet-era car rusting on the hillside behind them. An elderly woman smiles tenderly as she feeds pigeons. A child stands on his hands in a field of wildflowers. A loose puppy plays with a watermelon. A horse grazes on grass dotted with poppies before the expanse of a lake. Water asserts itself, gradually, as a recurring, calming presence. Like breath itself.

From beneath a glass table, on which rest an Ottoman lamp, a jug, and a coloured glass, the artist frames a blonde woman, an apparition against a blue sky. This inverted vantage point, where everything seems weightless, conveys less a place or a face than a state of grace. It seems to answer the “humanity” the artist says she has found here, and “the bright gravity” of the people she meets.

In the book’s final images, at the edge of a lake, a scarlet streak and a scattering of empty Coca-Cola bottles stain the crystalline water and its shore. Dye, or blood? The question is left hanging, much like the past itself, forever poised to resurface.

Mountain Black Heart (2026) by Irina Rozovsky is published by Mack and available for $75.
items.excerpt: The American photographer of Russian origin lets herself drift through the countries of former Yugoslavia and their neighbours. Published by Mack, Mountain Black Heart oscillates between unease and wonder, borne along by an unsettled familiarity with these territories.

items.title: Camille Vivier Sculpts the Flesh
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Camille Vivier Sculpts the Flesh

Only a few days remain to discover the first major retrospective the Maison Européenne de la Photographie devotes to Camille Vivier in Paris. A mesmerising journey in which bodybuilders, puppets and votive candles vie for the title of most beautiful living sculpture.


By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Camille Vivier.

For over twenty-five years, Camille Vivier’s eye has moved with rare fluency between fashion commissions and fine-art photography, two facets of a single obsession: probing what, within a body, already borders on statuary. Beginning her career in the late 1990s, she has forged a body of work in which glamour never stops flirting with the uncanny, where classical beauty is always shadowed by a whiff of unease.

At the heart of this retrospective reigns the female nude, unfurled through figures who have shaken the very foundations of conventional femininity. Sophie, Tjiki, Deborah: three bodybuilders with spectacular musculature, captured in stagings where the body reveals itself as raw material to be sculpted, a living architecture that rivals marble torsos.

One cannot help but think of the portraits Robert Mapplethorpe made of Lisa Lyon, who became the first world champion of women’s bodybuilding in 1979 and went on to be the American photographer’s muse in the 1980s, a direct wellspring for the “Sophie” series, born of the same fascination with anatomies that confound the assignment of gender.

The exhibition also unleashes an entire bestiary of anthropomorphic objects, summoned as much for their symbolic weight as their sheer visual strangeness: ritual candles drawn from Afro-Brazilian traditions, avant-garde puppets by Luigi Veronesi, a leading figure of 1930s Italian abstraction, biomechanical sets inherited from the world of H.R. Giger, the Swiss artist behind the creature in Alien.

This sweeping journey through nearly a hundred works, gelatin silver and digital prints, Polaroids, pieces conceived especially for the occasion, paints the portrait of an artist for whom photography remains, above all, a tool of illusion and metamorphosis, where the animate and the inanimate carry on a thoroughly illicit correspondence.

 

 

 

The exhibition “Camille Vivier” runs at the MEP in Paris, France, until September 13, 2026.

items.title: “Let’s Celebrate!”: Everyone’s Own Party, a Party for All
items.content:
Two faces all but disappear behind a flurry of multicoloured fans, caught mid-motion in a gesture that owes as much to dance as to parade. The scene could pass for a Magnum dispatch, so squarely does it favour a perfect composition. It was, in fact, taken in 2019, by a photographer nobody, a year earlier, had ever heard of. That is the whole premise of “Let’s Celebrate!”: blur the generations and keep only the moment.

Confetti

YellowKorner turned twenty, and has spent those twenty years defending one conviction: photography deserves to be shared, for everyone’s pleasure, and has no business staying locked inside contemporary art fairs. Twenty years spent opening galleries everywhere, from Bordeaux to Shanghai (eighty of them today), offering fine-art prints to private buyers and collectors alike. To mark the occasion, the house set photographers a simple brief: send us your celebration, the real one, yours, with your partner, your friends, your family, the one from your hometown, from your happiest moments.

What strikes you first is that no two images look alike. Some chose celebration in its most literal sense: crowds, confetti, paper streamers. Others preferred to render it obliquely: a solitary body, a beam of light, a held breath. The selection embraces that range, as if the word “celebration” only made sense in the plural. There is pure documentary alongside near-choreographed gesture, street and studio, saturated colour and austere black and white. The thread, thin but real, is a shared urgency: each photographer seems to have wanted to capture something that, a second later, would already be gone.

The geography, meanwhile, reads like a trip around the world in twenty frames. Alexandra Buxbaum checks in from Arizona, Olesia Kim from Tyumen, Eleonora Laufer from Buenos Aires, Yevhen Samuchenko from Odessa. In Brighton, Liban Elmi captured three boys wading into the sea arm in arm, backs to the camera, caught in the same motion. “Laughter crosses borders more easily than words,” the photographer wrote in his application, a line that alone sums up the spirit of the series. In Nandgaon, Vivek Goyal plunged into clouds of coloured powder during the Holi festival, where men and women douse each other until the pigment erases every face. “Colour becomes the ageless language of human connection,” he wrote. In Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer, Roxane Mo captured another register of celebration, closer to carnival than ritual: in “Flamboyer” (“Blaze”), a woman in a sequinned dress screams with joy under an orange hoop, surrounded by a costumed parade at the Pete the Monkey eco-festival. The image, an emblem of the series, sums up on its own what the whole selection is after: collective joy, unfiltered, full of colour and expression.

Memory

Head down a floor into the YellowKorner space, and an entirely different season opens up, more intimate: the season of memory sold at the counter. “Colorful,” the cult collection that built YellowKorner’s finest hours, has been reissued and expanded for a confidential, exclusive edition: twenty images to choose from, each delivered in its own dedicated case. Laurent Baheux returns with his African animals, in black and white, without an ounce of sentimentality. Matthieu Ricard suspends a Tibetan monk in meditation, outside of time, precisely what the La Hune gallery upstairs is celebrating. Thibaud Poirier files away his Trinity College library, a paper temple that could almost pass for a nave. Also featured: Formento+Formento, Pedro Jarque Krebs, Tull & Bruno Morandi, Nicolas Velter, Jakub Polomski, Bernhard Hartmann, Ruslan Bolgov, Ludwig Favre, Nicolas Bets, LDK, Fabien Novarino, Alexandre Fauve, Damien Dufresne, Robbie McIntosh, Mina Mimbu, Andrea Pavan. A roster of names whose prints are often sold out, now available again, ready to hang on your own wall.

Round Dance

Back in the exhibition, what still stands out is the absence of hierarchy between names you know and names you’re discovering. YellowKorner has always defended the idea that photography deserves to be accessible to everyone. The hang makes that case almost literally: no caption reveals who already had a career and who is just starting one. Laurent Paillier, who photographs dancers carved out by coloured light in an echo of Lucio Fontana slashing his canvases, may put it best: “It celebrates the living body, dance as a form of absolute happiness, light as a metaphor for life, and gesture as an act of freedom.” It should be added that this celebration reads less like a retrospective than a prologue. YellowKorner is changing face, reinventing its artistic direction, opening its doors wider to women photographers, to documentary approaches, to aesthetics owing less and less to the male gaze that long dominated the genre. Twenty years on, and the next chapter is already being written, somewhere between a case being closed and a fan unfolding.

“Let’s Celebrate!”, exhibition at La Hune gallery, Paris, September 19 to October 10, 2026. Opening night September 24, 2026. “Colorful” collection, on view in the YellowKorner-La Hune space on the ground floor, September 16 to October 14, 2026. All “Let’s Celebrate!” photographs are available for purchase on the YellowKorner website.

items.title: Visa pour l’Image: The World we “Must Keep Looking at”
items.content:
Thank you. Stephan Vanfleteren’s 2018 portrait of Jean-François Leroy is everywhere in Perpignan. Thirty-eight years ago, he co-founded what has become an unmissable gathering for the photojournalism family. He died on August 31, two days after the opening of this year’s edition of Visa pour l’image, “his baby.” He was 69.

That same evening, at the festival’s ritual opening screening at the Campo Santo, the 2,500 spectators in attendance rose to their feet. Long applause followed. French President Emmanuel Macron paid tribute in a statement to “the memory of a passionate journalist,” “a tireless defender of photojournalism.”

“A tribute he would have said he didn’t care about, but that he would have bragged about every two minutes,” smiled Delphine Lelu, his longtime associate, visibly moved. She and the rest of the festival’s team are picking up where he left off. “We will keep Visa alive in keeping with the values Jean-François defended.”

“A visual culture melting pot”

This year again, Visa pour l’image proved itself the crossroads of the profession: the place where people gather over a drink at the Café de la Poste, between two exhibitions at the Église des Dominicains, in the warmth of the halls at the Couvent des Minimes, or at the evening screenings to see colleagues’ work. Visa is a place of fellowship among people of the image.

In his legacy book, Le Devoir de regarder (The Duty to Look), Jean-François Leroy said as much: “This visual culture melting pot means that, every year, photographers, who are solitary the rest of the year, meet, look at each other, and exchange, from the most established to the beginners.”

Thus Raymond Depardon, a towering figure who had never before exhibited on Perpignan’s walls, appeared alongside a younger generation: Jerôme Gence, Robin Tutenges, Elise Blanchard, and Philémon Barbier. A happy mix, mutual admiration between two eras, a passing of the torch between generations. “Visa pour l’image’s mantra, for thirty-eight years, has remained the same: discovering young photographers, confirming and highlighting the work of established ones, and rediscovering ‘historic’ photographers of the past,” Jean-François Leroy wrote in his book.

In a profession whose economy is more precarious than ever, Visa is a lighthouse in the dark, a vital source of support. “What matters most to us is distributing 21 awards worth more than 160,000 euros. That’s serious help toward production,” Delphine Lelu points out.

Holding onto the truth

For nearly forty years, more than 220,000 visitors have come to look the world in the face (see this year’s full program here), taking the time to move from photo to photo, reading every introductory text, every caption. “Jean-François Leroy stood for holding onto the truth. That was all that mattered to him. He cared about showing the world as it is, without filters, while also making sure the information could reach as wide a public as possible,” Delphine Lelu recalls.

Coming to Visa means facing the gaze of young Afghan girls sold into marriage to support their families (Elise Blanchard), of virtual unions in Japan with manga characters (Jérôme Gence), diving into the depths of the oceans (Laurent Ballesta) as much as into the bowels of Chernobyl (Gerd Ludwig). It means confronting the news head-on: the agony of civilians in Gaza, the terror of drones in Ukraine, the forgotten wars of Ethiopia, Cambodia, or Sudan. It means putting a face to numbers: 1.5 million people affected by illiteracy in France (Jérémy Lempin), illustrating a geography, that of cocaine (Mads Nissen) or the exile of young Guinean minors (Hervé Lequeux).

Coming to Visa pour l’image means seeing the world at its worst, but also at its best. A world we “must keep looking at, even when looking at it is uncomfortable,” as Jean-François Leroy put it.

“AI has made authentic images suspect”

Visa has often been shunned by institutional circles. Ministerial visits are rare, and subsidies are meager compared with those given to the Rencontres d’Arles. “Visa pour l’image, that’s just boom-boom stuff,” one advisor at the Ministry of Culture once said. No comment.

As photography marks its bicentennial, the Perpignan festival reminds us every year that photojournalism cannot be treated as a lesser genre of the medium. Quite the opposite: this has been Visa’s fight since its first edition, in 1989. Jean-François Leroy put it in his own way: “As if photographing a war, a family, or a revolution were somehow less noble than photographing a lemon on a table.”

Visa serves the public good. The festival’s mission to educate people on how to look and how to understand information has never been more essential than today. In the age of artificial intelligence, generated images, and deepfakes, learning to look has become a societal priority. “AI has made authentic images suspect by contamination,” Jean-François Leroy warned.

The festival’s week dedicated to schoolchildren is precious. It should be extended to every school, given how vital the stakes are. Forewarned is forearmed. “I maintain that Visa pour l’image’s greatest value today is this education of the eye that we strive to uphold. Younger generations need to learn how to look, because soon, as adults and citizens, it will be their duty to do so,” Jean-François Leroy wrote.

An education through images that mattered so much to him, as did his support for the new generation of photographers. “Your camera doesn’t make you a photojournalist. Your ability to build a story with a series of images that have a beginning, a middle, and an end, that’s what makes you a photojournalist,” he wrote in a letter that now reads as a kind of testament. To pass it on so that photojournalism and its values endure, so that Visa pour l’image continues to bear witness to the world, so that we can keep looking at it as it truly is.

38th International Photojournalism Festival of Perpignan, Visa pour l’image, until September 13, 2026.

*« Le Devoir de regarder. Histoires et réflexions sur le photojournalisme » (The Duty to Look: Stories and Reflections on Photojournalism), Jean-François Leroy in conversation with Isabelle Fougère, is is published by Éditions Mkf and available for €20.
items.excerpt: The 38th edition of the international photojournalism festival in Perpignan was marked by mourning, following the death of its co-founder, Jean-François Leroy. An essential rendezvous for the profession, Visa pour l’image continues to teach us to look the world in the face.
